limitations: Native restrictions take precedence. Hook activation requires runtime trust.

Synced role definitions are projected to Codex agent files and can be listed as spawn_agent agent types. Listing a role does not qualify its execution or provide Claude Code subagent records; native acceptance checks role discovery separately.
Unsupported controls remain visible; custom stance prose does not add enforcement.

The usage feed is uncovered: this runtime raises none of UserPromptSubmit, SubagentStart or SubagentStop, so turn spend, the fresh-session nudge, in-flight width and finished-subagent spend are not fed back and no such event is registered.

Cache-prefix stability is not measurable here: this runtime reports a cached-read figure and no cache-write figure at all, so a ledger row carries real cached_input_tokens in cache_read and leaves cache_write unreported. `harness usage --by prefix` reports a Codex session as unknown rather than as a perfectly held prefix.

Return measurement is uncovered: this runtime writes a subagent to a rollout file of its own and records no parent-side tool use id on the child, so nothing joins a return to its call. A Codex subagent row records return_path, return_over_budget and return_measured as null, and `harness usage --by role` counts it in neither share.

Band routing is not decided on this runtime, so the decision log records no tier-agent-spawns row here: the spawn hook that reroutes an unnamed spawn to a band worker runs on Claude Code alone. Every other decision point writes on both runtimes, and the Bash ask is labelled from PostToolUse and SessionEnd, which both raise.

The completion claim on a stop-gate row is unverified here. The reader parses this runtime's rollout shape and accepts the three names its Stop payload could give the file, but no Codex Stop payload has been observed on the machine this was measured on. A row written here may therefore carry "completion_claim": null with "completion_claim_miss": "no_transcript_path", which is exactly this gap and is distinguishable from a transcript that was named and could not be read. The switch, the cap and the hash behave identically on both runtimes.

The intent-overlap check is uncovered at edit time: this runtime raises no PreToolUse for a file edit, so an edit to a path a live sibling has claimed is neither warned nor denied as it happens. The builder brief carries the claim step, and the gate runs `harness intent check` before commit, which exits non-zero on another session's overlap under the default `deny` variant and writes the same intent-overlap row.
